name: openslide
desc: C library to read whole-slide images (a.k.a. virtual slides)
why: Reads gigapixel pathology whole-slide images, a real scientific format door into digital microscopy.

brief.what_it_is: OpenSlide is a C library that gives programmers one simple interface for reading whole-slide images, also called virtual slides, which are very large high-resolution pathology scans. It takes in vendor files in a range of formats (Aperio .svs, Hamamatsu .ndpi, Leica .scn, MIRAX .mrxs, Zeiss .czi, DICOM, generic tiled TIFF, and others) and lets callers read tiles and regions at chosen resolutions without loading the whole image into RAM. It also exposes ICC profiles, textual metadata, and associated images such as a label and thumbnail. Python and Java bindings are published separately; the Python binding includes a Deep Zoom generator and a simple web viewer, and the Java binding includes a simple image viewer.
brief.why_it_exists: Whole-slide images routinely exceed RAM and are stored in vendor-specific formats that are often undocumented and usually readable only with a vendor's own Windows tools. The homepage frames OpenSlide as a vendor-neutral foundation so doctors and researchers are not tied to one vendor's viewer, and so non-Windows platforms can read these files.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internals in detail. It describes a C API with a consistent interface over the many vendor formats, and points to the API reference and per-format pages on the website for specifics. The 2013 Journal of Pathology Informatics paper linked from the homepage describes the design and implementation.

commands_seen.context: Configures a build directory for compiling OpenSlide from source; first step of the README's build instructions.
Compiles the source in the build directory created by meson setup.
Installs the compiled OpenSlide from the build directory into the system.

brief.install_notes: Building from source needs GCC or Clang, Meson, cairo >= 1.2, glib >= 2.56, libdicom >= 1.3 (built automatically if missing), libjpeg-turbo >= 1.3 or libjpeg >= 9c, libpng, libtiff >= 4.0, libxml2, OpenJPEG >= 2.1, SQLite >= 3.14, zlib, and Zstandard. The homepage also links a Windows usage guide and offers binary builds (version 4.0.1.2 is the latest listed). No accounts or hardware are needed. The Homebrew entry lists four executables (openslide-quickhash1sum, openslide-show-properties, openslide-write-png, slidetool), but neither fetched page documents them, so their usage is unverified.
brief.standout: It is a real scientific-format door into digital microscopy: it reads gigapixel pathology scans that most image libraries cannot open, and it was built by reverse-engineering vendor formats that were never documented. It comes from Satyanarayanan's group at Carnegie Mellon, and the website also hosts a web-based demo that renders several slide formats.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists OpenSlide 4.0.1 released 2026-06-07, with binary build 4.0.1.2 dated 2026-06-19, plus Python 1.4.6 and Java 0.13.3 releases on 2026-06-07. The news list shows steady releases through 2025 and 2026, and development happens on GitHub with separate issue trackers.
brief.caveats: Vendor support is not endorsed by the vendors and may be incomplete, per the homepage. The README says it reads brightfield slides only. The license is LGPL 2.1, so linking rules apply. Building from source requires many dependencies, and the build is heavier than a typical C library. The Homebrew entry has no caveats, and the executables it lists are not described in the fetched pages.
quotes: OpenSlide is a C library for reading whole slide image files (also known as virtual slides).
It provides a consistent and simple API for reading files from multiple vendors.
Whole-slide images routinely exceed RAM sizes, often occupying tens of gigabytes when uncompressed.
Vendors typically do not document their formats.
